title: Decision boundaries
use_cases: Use when defining structural constraints for genre-specific narratives
Implement when auditing a manuscript for reader expectation alignment
Configure when establishing world-building rules and internal consistency systems
Use when distinguishing between negotiable stylistic choices and mandatory plot requirements
content:
The practical question for any writer working in genre fiction is where the negotiable elements end and the non-negotiables begin.

Romance's non-negotiable is the happy ending — or at minimum, a "happy for now." Breaking that isn't subversion; it's a category error that produces reader betrayal. Mystery's non-negotiable is fair-play: the solution must be discoverable from clues the reader had access to. Science fiction's non-negotiable is internal consistency — the rules of the fictional universe apply even when inconvenient to the plot.

What is negotiable: narrative voice, point of view, pacing, thematic complexity, character depth, theme and symbolism, and how conventionally the genre's secondary elements are handled. A mystery can have experimental structure. A fantasy novel can skip the traditional hero's journey entirely.

Genre fiction is not a lesser form of fiction — it is, statistically, most of what people actually read. Writers considering where their work fits in the broader creative landscape benefit from understanding genre conventions not as constraints but as the inherited architecture of reader-writer collaboration, refined over more than a century of commercial storytelling.
